messages.body_plain:
Perhaps you can check out the 'ZIP and ZAP models' tutorial at the inlabru website: https://github.com/inlabru-org/inlabru (search in articles). This includes some Bayesian model check tools.

On Wed, 31 Jan 2024 at 18:41, Ciar Noble <ciar...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hello Elias,
>
> Thanks very much for your response, so the issue isn't with the spatial term per se, more so the combination of a binomial model and my data. That makes a lot of sense. Really, I'm not interested in the number of cells vs the number of trials, I'm interested in the proportion burnt, for which beta regression is more appropriate. However, as I have a large number of 0 values, this means I'd have to use a zero-inflated beta. To my understanding, if I were to use zero-inflated beta and include a spatial effect in the linear predictor for the mean of the beta distribution, this would not consider spatial autocorrelation among sites where the proportion burnt was > 0 and those where the proportion burnt = 0, which seems really important. Is this interpretation correct, and if so is there any way to fit a zero-inflated beta where autocorrelation is considered among sites with and without fire? I'm aware of this model (https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.07249), which I tried to implement in STAN but struggled to get working.
>
> Also, what test for spatial sutocorrelation would be more appropriate?
>
> Thanks again,
>
> Ciar
>
> On Wednesday, January 31, 2024 at 2:43:17 PM UTC Elias T. Krainski wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > The primary reason to see such a result is because you have big Ntrials and so the posterior has more information from the data than from the prior. Thus, as soon as you allow a different probability for each observation, the posterior looks like the data likelihood.
> >
> > If you want to try having correlate spatial effects over time one way is to consider a term like
> >    f(Landcape_ID, model = 'besag', graph = my_graph2, group = Year, control.group = list(model = 'ar1'))
> >
> > Having one parameter for each time will just allow more flexibility, and it seems that you want the opposite.
> >
> > I would not consider this kind of Moran test for this kind of 'residuals'...
> >
> > best regards,
> > Elias
> >
> >
> > On Tue, 30 Jan 2024 at 20:15, Ciar Noble <ciar...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Hello,
> > >
> > > I'm very new to INLA so forgive me if parts of my question are already answered.
> > >
> > > I am trying to model the influence of landscape composition on the extent of forest fires in the Amazon. I have 34 years of data and have divided my region into a 10 x 10 km grid/lattice. I've calculated the total number of forest raster cells in each grid cell and the number of these forest cells that were burnt, in each of the 34 year. I am then using binomial regression to model the proportion of forest cells burnt.
> > >
> > > I am not so interested in any temporal effects, and have included a variety of climatic variables as covariates that should, in theory, account for any such trends. However, as fires are highly seasonal, I only wish to incorporate spatial autocorrelation among sites within years. Thus, I have been generating one overarching queen's case adjacency matrix, where cells can only be considered neighbours with cells from the same year.
> > >
> > > I created a non-spatial model, the residuals of which exhibit substantial spatial autocorrelation (Moran’s I ranges from 0.1 – 0.8 within years). I’ve then trialled a variety of spatial terms with this model, namely the ‘besag’, ‘besagproper’ and ‘bym’.  However, all methods lead to extreme overfitting. For example, the fitted vs true proportion of forest burnt from the ‘besag’ model:
> > >
> > >
> > > I’m not sure why this is, as the precision parameters of the spatial terms are not unreasonably high, e.g., the precision of the ‘besag’ term is 0.04 ± 0.001. Furthermore, there is still spatial autocorrelation in the residuals (according to Moran's I), although it is reduced compared to the non-spatial model.
> > >
> > > One thing I can think of is that as well as there being notable spatial autocorrelation in the response, there is similar clustering in all the predictor variables within each year. I’m not entirely sure how this may effect the estimation of spatial autocorrelation terms.
> > >
> > > If I fit a model considering spatial autocorrelation across years, the overfitting problem is resolved. However, this doesn't align with how I'd expect the spatial dynamics of fire to operate within the landscape, especially since this is, in theory, relating response values from one year to response values from neighbouring cells in the future. Nonetheless, am I perhaps wrong to focus on spatial autocorrelation within years, and instead should be attributing intra-annual variation in fire entirely to the spatial clustering of the year-specific predictor variables?
> > >
> > > I'm wonder if I should instead try to estimate seperate random effects (with separate variance terms) for each year? However, I'm not sure how I'd go about this in INLA.
> > >
> > > Ultimately my questions are: Are they any likely reasons why the model is overfitting to such an extreme extent, but not fully dealing with the autocorrelation? And is there perhaps a more appropriate method to account for spatial autocorrelation in this situation?
> > >
> > > I have uploaded the data and code to do the analyses I've already tried to this drive folder https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1FfcTBPqV5gYiRxCi4Wji5L_XG22NKc9k?usp=drive_link
> > >
> > > Thanks for any help,
> > >
> > > Ciar

messages.subject: Issues with WAIC and DIC calculations in integrated SDM
messages.subject_clean: Issues with WAIC and DIC calculations in integrated SDM
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

Myself and a few others have been encountering issues when using the PointedSDMs package (based on inlabru - https://github.com/PhilipMostert/PointedSDMs) to fit integrated species distribution models. Our models have been producing WAIC values which are "-Inf" or "NaN", or which are extremely large (e.g. 2.56e+182). The DIC values for these models also tend to be NA. The issue does not appear to be confined to a particular dataset or specific covariates.

We have been discussing the issue over on GitHub (https://github.com/PhilipMostert/PointedSDMs/issues/5) but haven't yet managed to pinpoint the cause, so I thought I would also post here in case anybody is able to help.

An example with very large WAIC and DIC = NA can be reproduced using the Solitary Tinamou example dataset which comes with PointedSDMs:

library(PointedSDMs)
library(terra)

data("SolitaryTinamou")
projection <- "+proj=longlat +ellps=WGS84"
species <- SolitaryTinamou$datasets
NPP <- scale(terra::rast(system.file('extdata/SolitaryTinamouCovariates.tif',
                                     package = "PointedSDMs"))$NPP)
mesh <- SolitaryTinamou$mesh

model <- intModel(species, spatialCovariates = NPP, Coordinates = c('X', 'Y'),
                  Projection = projection, Mesh = mesh, responsePA = 'Present')
modelRun <- fitISDM(model, options = list(control.inla = list(int.strategy = 'eb'),
                                          safe = TRUE))

The model output from this example is:

Summary of 'bruSDM' object: inlabru version: 2.10.1 INLA version: 23.09.09 Types of data modelled: eBird Present only Parks Present absence Gbif Present only Time used: Pre = 5.28, Running = 277, Post = 0.38, Total = 283 Fixed effects: mean sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant mode kld NPP 13.595 0.455 12.704 13.595 14.485 13.595 0 eBird_intercept -16.881 1.910 -20.624 -16.881 -13.138 -16.881 0 Parks_intercept -22.089 2.001 -26.010 -22.089 -18.168 -22.089 0 Gbif_intercept -18.490 1.913 -22.240 -18.490 -14.741 -18.490 0 Random effects: Name Model shared_spatial SPDE2 model Model hyperparameters: mean sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant mode Theta1 for shared_spatial -2.36 0.008 -2.37 -2.36 -2.34 -2.37 Theta2 for shared_spatial -5.82 0.013 -5.84 -5.82 -5.79 -5.84 Deviance Information Criterion (DIC) ...............: NA Deviance Information Criterion (DIC, saturated) ....: NA Effective number of parameters .....................: NA Watanabe-Akaike information criterion (WAIC) ...: 4.64e+39 Effective number of parameters .................: 2.32e+39 Marginal log-Likelihood: -790.12 is computed Posterior summaries for the linear predictor and the fitted values are computed (Posterior marginals needs also 'control.compute=list(return.marginals.predictor=TRUE)')

Many thanks,
Peter

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Issues with WAIC and DIC calculations in integrated SDM
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Issues with WAIC and DIC calculations in integrated SDM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Peter,

since WAIC is related to leave-one-out cross-validation (see e.g.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/1507.04544.pdf which I think has since been
published), it is not a well-defined concept for point process models,
where the continuous _space_ (together with the individual points) is
the "observation". The likelihood construction in inlabru is not based
on spatial gridding and aggregating counts (which would yield a
poisson count model as the approximate model, for which WAIC would be
well defined) but rather a higher order approximation method. Work is
underway for a more well-defined cross-validation quantity, but as it
is, WAIC is not appropriate to use for general point process models,
whether in inla/inlabru or other software. Only basic aggregation
approximations have well defined WAIC quantities.
(Note: earlier materials for inlabru did compute WAIC, since we hadn't
realised the problem with how WAIC is defined, or rather not defined
at all, in this context!)

For DIC, the situation _should_ be better, but I suspect that one
would need to keep more careful track of normalisation constants.
Until someone has time to do the necessary maths&coding, I prefer
other model assessment methods based on more explicit spatially
resolved prediction evaluation. See for example the point process
residuals vignette at
https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/2d_lgcp_residuals.html

There have also been other recent work on point process forecast
assessments; usually these are based on prediction of aggregated
counts on a specific spatial scale.
The vignette on prediction score computation with inlabru,
https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/prediction_scores.html,
doesn't cover point processes explicitly, but it does cover count
models, which can be applied to point process predictions.

When working with point processes, one has to be mindful that the
observations are of a fundamentally different nature than for
point-referenced observations at given locations, and the usual
turnkey solutions don't always apply!

Finn

messages.subject: Modelling circular data in INLA
messages.subject_clean: Modelling circular data in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I'm investigating whether it'll be possible to fit simple models to circular data in INLA. I see that two circular distributions are available in INLA: 'circularnormal' and 'wrappedcauchy'. In INLA it seems that the circular normal distribution has experimental status only, while the wrapped Cauchy distribution is disabled. How experimental is the circular normal distribution in INLA? Should it be used at all?

I tried the simplest possible model - just finding the mean of some circular data - and it didn't seem to work.
> require(INLA)
> require(circular) #For rvonmises
> test_df<-data.frame("angle"=as.numeric(rvonmises(1000,5,2)))
> mean(test_df$angle) [1] 4.581486
> hist(test_df$angle)

> model_circ<-inla(angle~1,family ="circularnormal",data=test_df)
> summary(model_circ)
Call: c("inla.core(formula = formula, family = family, contrasts = contrasts, ", " data = data, quantiles = quantiles, E = E, offset = offset, ", " scale = scale, weights = weights, Ntrials = Ntrials, strata = strata, ", " lp.scale = lp.scale, link.covariates = link.covariates, verbose = verbose, ", " lincomb = lincomb, selection = selection, control.compute = control.compute, ", " control.predictor = control.predictor, control.family = control.family, ", " control.inla = control.inla, control.fixed = control.fixed, ", " control.mode = control.mode, control.expert = control.expert, ", " control.hazard = control.hazard, control.lincomb = control.lincomb, ", " control.update = control.update, control.lp.scale = control.lp.scale, ", " control.pardiso = control.pardiso, only.hyperparam = only.hyperparam, ", " inla.call = inla.call, inla.arg = inla.arg, num.threads = num.threads, ", " keep = keep, working.directory = working.directory, silent = silent, ", " inla.mode = inla.mode, safe = FALSE, debug = debug, .parent.frame = .parent.frame)" ) Time used: Pre = 0.52, Running = 5.6, Post = 0.139, Total = 6.26 Fixed effects: mean sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant mode kld (Intercept) 739.196 578.952 263.942 517.286 2493.135 497.099 0.443 Model hyperparameters: mean sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant mode Precision parameter for the Circular Normal observations 0.002 0.003 0.00 0.001 0.011 0.00 Marginal log-Likelihood: -1843.69 is computed Posterior summaries for the linear predictor and the fitted values are computed (Posterior marginals needs also 'control.compute=list(return.marginals.predictor=TRUE)')

As you can see, the estimate of the mean (739) is way off, and the precision seems very low. Fitting a non-circular model, with a Normal error structure, is much more able:
> model_noncirc<-inla(angle~1,family ="gaussian",data=test_df) > summary(model_noncirc)  Call: c("inla.core(formula = formula, family = family, contrasts = contrasts, ", " data = data, quantiles = quantiles, E = E, offset = offset, ", " scale = scale, weights = weights, Ntrials = Ntrials, strata = strata, ", " lp.scale = lp.scale, link.covariates = link.covariates, verbose = verbose, ", " lincomb = lincomb, selection = selection, control.compute = control.compute, ", " control.predictor = control.predictor, control.family = control.family, ", " control.inla = control.inla, control.fixed = control.fixed, ", " control.mode = control.mode, control.expert = control.expert, ", " control.hazard = control.hazard, control.lincomb = control.lincomb, ", " control.update = control.update, control.lp.scale = control.lp.scale, ", " control.pardiso = control.pardiso, only.hyperparam = only.hyperparam, ", " inla.call = inla.call, inla.arg = inla.arg, num.threads = num.threads, ", " keep = keep, working.directory = working.directory, silent = silent, ", " inla.mode = inla.mode, safe = FALSE, debug = debug, .parent.frame = .parent.frame)" ) Time used: Pre = 0.482, Running = 0.513, Post = 0.164, Total = 1.16 Fixed effects: mean sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant mode kld (Intercept) 4.581 0.041 4.5 4.581 4.663 4.581 0 Model hyperparameters: mean sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant mode Precision for the Gaussian observations 0.587 0.026 0.536 0.586 0.639 0.586 Marginal log-Likelihood: -1700.98 is computed Posterior summaries for the linear predictor and the fitted values are computed (Posterior marginals needs also 'control.compute=list(return.marginals.predictor=TRUE)')

Please let me know what approach you'd recommend for fitting models to circular response data in INLA. Many thanks,
Jacob

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I've been successfully running integrated species distribution models for a few weeks using package pointedSDMs until yesterday/today. I reran a few lines of code today and a whole series of breakdowns seem to be happening, but specifically when fitting models with spatial covariates which are a RasterStack. I have triple checked the covariates align spatially with the observation data, mesh, and rasters have same extent, resolution and projection (and these were running fine until recently).  I have current version of R (v. 4.3.2) and all loaded packages are updated.

Wondering if this is an issue with rgdal (v. 1.6-7) /sp (v. 2.1-3) /inlabru (v. 2.10.1) / pointedSDMs (v.1.3.1) - and if others have encountered this and have solutions to offer? I feel like it's an rgdal issue but I don't have enough info to back up this statement.

Hopefully my description was clear enough :\

What I ran to give me error (Error: [extract] raster has no values)

> full2 <- PointedSDMs::intModel(data,
+                                spatialCovariates = covariates, # RasterStack;
+                                Coordinates = c('X', 'Y'),  # lat/long;

+                                responseCounts = 'Count',

messages.subject: Specifying spatial random effects with multiple likelihoods
messages.subject_clean: Specifying spatial random effects with multiple likelihoods
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA experts,

I am trying to create a multivariate mixture of Gaussians using INLA combined with AMIS. To do so, I am fitting a model using multiple likelihoods as described in several publications by Virgilio Gómez-Rubio and others. Given K mixture components and D variables, I calling the inla()-function with K*D repeated Gaussians in the ""family" argument.

Now I want to try and replicate another model I found in the literature. It uses univariate CAR spatial effects for each component to estimate the mixture weights. There's also a multivariate CAR effect in there, which I am implementing from the INLAMSM package. This MCAR effect is a specific wrapper around inla.rgeneric. It is configured through an argument "k" that's set to the number of variables. Using these spatial effects with my data structure for multiple likelihoods has become problematic.

Let n denote the number of observations. My code creates a matrix of size [D*n] by [K*D] right now. Throughout the AMIS algorithm repopulates the matrix, splitting each variable into it's specific component. After each iteration, the INLA model is fitted again to derive parameters for refining my estimates of the mixture component memberships. Here's a very basic example of what this matrix looks like with n=3, K=2, and D=3:

Using this matrix format, I can fit a Gaussian to each mixture component and variable. Yet I don't uinderstand how to add the spatial effects I just described. Would anyone know if and how I can correctly configure the inla()-function to couple the univariate and multivariate spatial effect to the right data columns? I looked into using inla.stack, copy, and replicate, but I can't wrap my head around how to make it work. Perhaps change something about how I use the "data" argument in the inla()-function? Or should I just change the format of my data matrix? Any ideas are greatly appreciated. Thank you in advance.

Best,

Bas Matsuura

If you want to have a random effect at a data row, give the index for it. If that line haven't that random effect, set the index of it to NA.

On Fri, 2 Feb 2024 at 22:04, Bas Matsuura <matsuu...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Dear INLA experts,
>
> I am trying to create a multivariate mixture of Gaussians using INLA combined with AMIS. To do so, I am fitting a model using multiple likelihoods as described in several publications by Virgilio Gómez-Rubio and others. Given K mixture components and D variables, I calling the inla()-function with K*D repeated Gaussians in the ""family" argument.
>
> Now I want to try and replicate another model I found in the literature. It uses univariate CAR spatial effects for each component to estimate the mixture weights. There's also a multivariate CAR effect in there, which I am implementing from the INLAMSM package. This MCAR effect is a specific wrapper around inla.rgeneric. It is configured through an argument "k" that's set to the number of variables. Using these spatial effects with my data structure for multiple likelihoods has become problematic.
>
> Let n denote the number of observations. My code creates a matrix of size [D*n] by [K*D] right now. Throughout the AMIS algorithm repopulates the matrix, splitting each variable into it's specific component. After each iteration, the INLA model is fitted again to derive parameters for refining my estimates of the mixture component memberships. Here's a very basic example of what this matrix looks like with n=3, K=2, and D=3:
>
>
>
> Using this matrix format, I can fit a Gaussian to each mixture component and variable. Yet I don't uinderstand how to add the spatial effects I just described. Would anyone know if and how I can correctly configure the inla()-function to couple the univariate and multivariate spatial effect to the right data columns? I looked into using inla.stack, copy, and replicate, but I can't wrap my head around how to make it work. Perhaps change something about how I use the "data" argument in the inla()-function? Or should I just change the format of my data matrix? Any ideas are greatly appreciated. Thank you in advance.
>
> Best,
>
> Bas Matsuura

Overall though, I'm content that things are working.

Scott

better.

Hi Everyone,

I am building a zero-inflated INLA model with spatial autocorrelation to assess seabird distribution. I went through Link_1 <https://github.com/florianhartig/DHARMa/issues/341>, and Link_2 <https://rdrr.io/cran/DHARMa/f/vignettes/DHARMa.Rmd> to try to understand how to simulate and analyse my residuals, but I don’t know how to apply this to myZero Inflated INLA spatial autocorrelation model. Could anyone guide me on how to use it, or if someone has already used it and would be willing to share the code? Attached please are my data and graphs to analyse.

I attached the model code, data, and Pearson's residuals graph.

messages.body_plain:
Hey all,

For inla(), there's a "scale" argument that takes information on the precision of the response variable. Is it possible to include this information using the bru() wrapper function? Using inla(), we supply the known precision (scale) and fix the likelihood precision to one as below:

result <- inla(y ~ x, data=dat1, scale=prec_y,
   control.family=list(hyper=list(prec=list(initial=1, fixed=TRUE))))

How would one do this in bru()? The control.family options would fall in the options argument as a list item I presume, but what about the "scale = prec_y" part?

Thank you,
Jordan

messages.subject_clean: Unexpected output for fixed effect given prior
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I attach a data csv and an R script containing a few lines of code to illustrate my issue. The modeling scenario is a standard football goals model where goals are modelled as:

y ~ Po(lambda) and
For home team: log(lambda) = home + attack_rating(own) + defence_rating(opp) ;
For away team: log(lambda) = attack_rating(own) + defence_rating(opp)

As such, home is a 1/0 indicator variable, indicating whether the team represented by the attack rating is the home team or not.

When I run the model using default priors, I get back expected output which is a mean value for home of the order of around 0.3.

Now in my real life case, I used this mean value together with the implied value for the precision (ie sd ^-2) as a prior for the subsequent season. When I did this, the mean value for the home parameter reduced to around half this expected value.

For the purposes of this example, I have plugged back in this prior into the same data set. And I observe a similar outcome. The mean value for the home parameter reduces to around half the expected value. And this is despite the precision of the prior being relatively high (around 320).

Can anyone explain?

messages.body_plain:
Hi Morgane,

I am not able to answer all your questions at the moment. But to get you started, there were some bugs in the example code you linked to. Here is some running code for a simple Poisson example.

Best,
Tim

# set up
library(INLA)
library(DHARMa)

# make data
dat = createData(sampleSize = 500, randomEffectVariance = 0)

# fit model
fit = inla(observedResponse ~ 1 + Environment1 , family = "poisson",
           data = dat,
           control.family=list(link='log'),
           control.predictor=list(link=1, compute=TRUE),
           control.compute=list(config = TRUE))
summary(fit)

# get and transform posterior samples
sim <- inla.posterior.sample(50, fit)
sim <- inla.posterior.sample.eval("Predictor", sim)
sim <- exp(sim) # need to exponentiate
poi <- function(x){
  x = ifelse(x<0, 0, x)
  rpois(1, x)
}
sim <- apply(sim, c(1,2), poi)

# run diagnostics
res <- createDHARMa(simulatedResponse=sim,
                    observedResponse=dat$observedResponse)
plot(res)

You're right, it looks a little puzzeling.

it seems like the cause the precision for the fixed effect.

I cannot see why you do not want constr=T also for 'def'.

I modified the priors for the precisions, but the overall results are
the same.

library(INLA)

data <- read.csv("data.csv")

prec.prior <- list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(0.5, 0.01)))

formula <- y ~ -1 + home + f(att, model = "iid", constr = T, hyper =
prec.prior) +
                f(def, model = "iid", constr = T, hyper = prec.prior)

fit <- inla(formula, data = data, family = "poisson")
summary(fit)

priorFixedEffect <- list(mean = fit$summary.fixed$mean, prec =
fit$summary.fixed$sd^-2)

fit2 <- inla(formula,
            data = data,
            control.fixed = priorFixedEffect,
            family = "poisson")
summary(fit2)

messages.body_plain:
there is no zero/one inflated for beta. since its continous, if you
observe 0 or 1, you know its inflated, so there is no need for one. you
can model the 0's and 1's directly (like with a binary regression) and
the non-0/1's with a beta. so a non-0/1 has two likelihood
contributions, its not 0 or 1, and then its beta.

beta likelihood takes data between 0 and 1, and you have to scale it
accordingly.

beta has also a trunctation argument for handliing cases near zero and 1
better, see the documentation

messages.body_plain:
its not that it cannot be done. its acutally a bit of work to do this
right. I do not like much the approach taken in that paper. it could be
done properly if needed, but some cencoring is needed at the end, as in
practice a reported 0 is not necessary a 0. also the behaviour near 0
and 1 will impact the parameterisation, as the density needs to be
somewhat continous near 0 and 1. like for Beta(a,a), we would need 'a <=
1' not to have zero density at the boundaries (before the inflated stuff
is added), which require a specialized parameterisation as the linear
predictor needs to be unconstrained.

its still possible to do not-to-bad with the multilikelihood approach,
with a logistic regression to be in the two tails, and then a beta model
inbetween.

which mean that in the interior, there is 3 likelihood contributions,
not in the 0 tail, not in the 1 tail and then in the beta interior.

in the left, its two, left tail and not in right tail. similar with the
right tail.

yes, it can be done...

messages.body_plain:
I apologize for my late reply.

Here is an executable example with the data attached:
With EMEP_air as a quantitative variable, Biogeo as a 4-factor quantitative variable, and Cd_mousse as my response variable.

library(dplyr)
library(inlabru)

load("~/df_example.Rdata")

df_sf <- df %>% sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE)

### model lm

model <- lm(log(Cd_mousse) ~ EMEP_air + Biogeo +EMEP_air:Biogeo, data = df)
summary(model)

model2 <- lm(log(Cd_mousse) ~ EMEP_air*Biogeo, data = df)
summary(model2)

### model bru

model_interaction_bru <- bru(log(Cd_mousse) ~ -1 +
                               my_fixed_effects(main = ~ EMEP_air + Biogeo + EMEP_air:Biogeo ,
                                                model = "fixed"),
                             family = "gaussian", data = df_sf)

model_interaction_bru$summary.random

model_interaction_bru2 <- bru(log(Cd_mousse) ~ -1 +
                                my_fixed_effects(main = ~ EMEP_air*Biogeo ,
                                                 model = "fixed"),
                              family = "gaussian", data = df_sf)

model_interaction_bru2$summary.random
inlaBru model and R's lm function of the stats package differ in estimated coefficients. (EMEP_air estimated to 25,72 with inlabru and 32.60 with lm)

I tried the same code with another dataset that meuse provides to the sp package, and the difference is not significant. As you said in your previous answer, the difference must be due to how the two packages estimate the coefficients; I had yet to pay attention to this.
Is it feasible to adjust the variance prior to aligning more closely with the solutions provided by the lm package in a fixed-effect model?

Thank you for your time and assistance.

--
Jérémy

Looking in particular at the parameters with large absolute deviation from zero, it seems clear to me that the differences are entirely between maximum likelihood and maximum posterior mode values, i.e. the difference between plain MaxLik frequentist estimation and posterior distributions in  Bayesian analysis. The sds are quite large, making the choice of prior distributions influential, and also pulling the point estimates towards zero, which is exactly what should be expected to happen.
Finn

messages.subject: Shared hyperprior across random effects for the same observation
messages.subject_clean: Shared hyperprior across random effects for the same observation
messages.body_plain:
What I would like to be able to do is share the same hyperprior across 2 different random effects for the same observation. Here's a contrived example.  The values of the random effects (group_var1 and group_var2) come from the same distribution but are different by group. I would like to be able to specify the same hyperprior in f() for both and for the model fit to similarly just return a single posterior (not one for each of Var1 and Var2). I've had a look into copy and replicate but I don't believe either suit my needs.

library(INLA)
n_groups <- 10
group <- letters[1:n_groups]

dat <- expand.grid(group, group)

dat <- dat %>% filter(Var1 != Var2)

set.seed(1)
group_var1 <- rnorm(n_groups, 0, 1)
group_var2 <- rnorm(n_groups, 0, 1)

y1 <- sapply(1:nrow(dat), function(z) group_var1[dat$Var1[z] == group])
y2 <- sapply(1:nrow(dat), function(z) group_var2[dat$Var2[z] == group])

dat$y <- y1 + y2

fit <- inla(y ~ -1 + f(Var1) + f(Var2), data = dat)

messages.subject_clean: Analysis of Residuals from ZAP INLA with spatial autocorrelation and DHARMa
messages.body_plain:
Once you get your sampling to work, here is some code for using DHARMa for ZIP data.

# make data for type I ZIP
n <- 100
p <- 0.8
lam <- 2
y <- rpois(n, lambda = lam)
y[rbinom(n, size=1, prob=p) == 1] = 0
dat1 <- data.frame(y=y)

# make model
mod1 <- inla(y ~ 1,
             family = "zeroinflatedpoisson1",
             data = dat1,
             control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
             control.compute=list(config=TRUE))
summary(mod1)

# get posterior samples of expectations and transforms to simulated counts
sim1 <- inla.posterior.sample(50, mod1)
sim1 <- inla.posterior.sample.eval("Predictor", sim1)
sim1 <- exp(sim1) # need exponentiation
marg1 <- mod1$marginals.hyperpar$`zero-probability parameter for zero-inflated poisson_1`
poi <- function(x, marg){
  p <- inla.rmarginal(1, marg)
  p <- 1 - p
  y <- rpois(1, x)
  y <- y * rbinom(1, size=1, prob=p)
  return(y)
}
sim1 <- apply(sim1, c(1, 2), poi, marg=marg1)

# run diagnostics in DHARMa
res <- createDHARMa(simulatedResponse=sim1,
                    observedResponse=dat1$y,
                    integerResponse = T)
plot(res)

messages.body_plain:
OK, here is a way to do it with all posterior samples, rather than using inla.rmarginal().

# make data
n <- 100
p <- 0.75

lam <- 2
y <- rpois(n, lambda = lam)
y[rbinom(n, size=1, prob=p) == 1] = 0
dat1 <- data.frame(y=y)

# make model
mod1 <- inla(y ~ 1,
             family = "zeroinflatedpoisson1",
             data = dat1,
             control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
             control.compute=list(config=TRUE))
summary(mod1)

# get posterior samples of p and lambda
ss1 <- 50
samps1 <- inla.posterior.sample(ss1, mod1)
get_p <- function(...){return(theta[1])}
sim_p <- inla.posterior.sample.eval(get_p, samps1)
sim_lam <- exp(inla.posterior.sample.eval("Predictor", samps1))

# use p and lambda samples to simulate counts
out_sim <- sim_lam
for(i in 1:nrow(sim_lam)){
  for(j in 1:ncol(sim_lam)){
    p <- sim_p[,j]

    p <- 1 - p

    y <- rpois(1, sim_lam[i,j])
    y <- y * rbinom(n=1, size=1, prob=p)
    out_sim[i, j] <- y

  }
}

# run diagnostics in DHARMa

res <- createDHARMa(simulatedResponse=out_sim,

                    observedResponse=dat1$y,
                    integerResponse = T)
plot(res)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Shared hyperprior across random effects for the same observation
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Shared hyperprior across random effects for the same observation
messages.body_plain:
You can do this by combining “replicate” with inla.stack() to let the predictor involve both replicates in a single response. That the two “replicates” don’t necessarily use the same number of elements doesn’t matter, as long as the model is long enough to accommodate both of them. The 2015 JSS paper on spatial modelling with INLA has a section about how inla.stack works, that will hopefully point you in the right direction of what you need to do. (Also, what you’re describing is not merely to have the _priors_ be the same, but rather to have the actual variance parameter itself be the same.)
Finn

I would like to be able to specify the same hyperprior in f() for both and for the model fit to similarly just return a single posterior (not one for each of Var1 and Var2). messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I’m unfortunately not familiar with the scale argument, so can’t tell you exactly, but I’m sure it’s not on log scale; it is a multiplicative scaling of some form. (Log-ing data just creates a new variable and inla doesn’t know that it came from some other variable. You have to define the model in terms of the response variable you do provide, so if you pre-log the data you have a different model)

If I recall correctly, inlabru detects control.family in the options and silently applies it to the observation model if there is only one observation model, but warns about a potential problem if it’s ambiguous which observation model it should be applied to.
In any case, supplying it to like() is the right thing to do.

Finn

messages.subject: A Modified Poisson Regression - Zhou et al Approach in R-INLA
messages.subject_clean: A Modified Poisson Regression - Zhou et al Approach in R-INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm exploring the implementation of a modified Poisson regression with robust variance, following the recommendation by Zhou et al. in 2004. This is particularly useful for modeling a binary outcome with a common prevalence ratio (PR).

In R, you can achieve this using the glm model and the sandwich package for robust variance. Here's an example:

library("sandwich")
library("lmtest")

model <- glm(outcome ~ exposure, family = poisson(link = log), data = dataset)
coeftest(model, vcov = sandwich)

This model, expressed as log(λ) = β₀ + β₁ ⋅ exposure, calculates standard errors with robust variance for more reliable results.

SErobust​(βi​)=V(βi​)√​

I'm curious if there's a way to implement this approach in the r-inla.

messages.subject: Fitting two datasets using non-sparse A-matrix and an RW2 model
messages.subject_clean: Fitting two datasets using non-sparse A-matrix and an RW2 model
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am currently looking to model two datasets simultaneously, where the second dataset is much more sparse (n2 << n1, rest is NA) and represent independent corrections of the first dataset. The goal is to infer potential structural biases in the first dataset using the observed values in the second dataset.

The first model uses fixed effects and an AR(1) component, the second is the cumulative sum of the first model with an additional RW2 component to represent a potential bias term.
My strategy is to use the A matrix to transform the predictor such that the second (RW2) component also includes a cumulative sum of the first component (this implies a non-sparse matrix A).

However, the dataset I am trying to fit is very large (~20,000), and I am unable to achieve numerical convergence for simulations even half that size.

Are there any possible tricks I could employ to help improve stability? Is it even feasible to do this in R-INLA? I have already tried using "inla.group". I have lots of patience so speed is secondary.

Here is a runnable simulation example which seem to work fine for small n (<=1000):

library(INLA)
set.seed(1991)
n = 20000 #approximately the length of the real data
z = seq(0, 3, length.out=n)

phi=0.4
y0 = arima.sim(list(ar=phi),n=n,sd=sqrt(1-phi^2))

y1 = seq(-1,1,length.out=n) + y0
y2 = cumsum(y1)+ 100 * sin(z)
y22 = rep(NA,n)

nobs = 5 #number of observations in y2
indices = sort(sample(1:n,nobs))

y22[indices] = y2[indices]
yy = c(y1,y22)
plot(yy)

formula = yy ~ -1 + fixed + trend + f(idx1,model="ar1") +
  f(idx2,model="rw2", constr=FALSE)
idx2 = c(rep(NA,n),1:n)

data=data.frame(yy=yy,
                fixed=c(rep(1,n),rep(1,n)),
                idx1 = c(1:n,1:n),
                trend=c(z,z),
                idx2=idx2 )

Imat = Diagonal(n,1)
Omat = Diagonal(n,0)
Rmat = Imat
Rmat[lower.tri(Rmat)] = 1 #cumulative sums

Amat = rbind( cbind(Imat, Omat), cbind(Rmat, Imat) )

r = inla(formula,data=data,family="gaussian", control.compute=list(config=TRUE),
         control.family = list(fixed=TRUE,initial=12),
         num.thread=1,
         control.predictor=list(A=Amat))
summary(r)

plot(yy, ylim=range(r$summary.linear.predictor$`0.025quant`, r$summary.linear.predictor$`0.975quant`))
lines(r$summary.linear.predictor$mean,col="blue")
lines(r$summary.linear.predictor$`0.025quant`,col="red")
lines(r$summary.linear.predictor$`0.975quant`,col="red")

I would be very grateful for any comments

Many thanks in advance

Eirik

and see how much of the cummilative sum that you really need. Although
the math says cummulative sum since beginning of time, I guess the
practice is different.

with the above I could easily run full data-size on my laptop. question
is how large you can make the '10' above. (and then you also need to be
smarter in defining a band matrix than I was....)

this large dense block is what is killing it. its not that you cannot do
it with that construction, more that the implementation is not ment for
these cases. we can do this with dense matrix algorithms (on several
machines using MPI) but that is not implemented (Although Esmail, cc'ed
in here, did this as a part of his PhD for a different set of models).

Havard

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am working with a proportional odds model using inla and I was wondering if you could provide more information on the prior for the intercept.

Here is a simple example of a model:

library(brms)
library(INLA)
data(inhaler)

inla_pom <- inla(rating ~ treat + period + carry, data = inhaler, family='pom',
                 control.family=list(hyper=list(theta1=list(prior="dirichlet", param=3))))
inla.priors.used(inla_pom)

Which gives me the following output:

Why is the Dirichlet prior only assigned to theta1?  Is it possible to assign a prior to theta2 and theta3?

I have read the following paper

https://inla.r-inla-download.org/r-inla.org/doc/likelihood/pom.pdf

but I don't understand how the reparameterization from alpha to theta works. Can you please offer additional information on this?

Thank you!

Abigail

messages.subject_clean: DIC in INLA and inlabru
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am fitting LGCP models and want to compare them using the DIC.
When I fit the same models using INLA and inlabru, and they usually yield very similar results, but the DIC is really different.

I linked an example (based on https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/spde-gitbook/ch-lcox.html#introduction-1) where I fit both models. The intercept, range and sigma are almost identical, but the DIC is -727.6 with INLA, and -67.22 with inlabru.

How do we explain this and is one of the DIC more reliable?

Thank you!

Edgar

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] DIC in INLA and inlabru
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] DIC in INLA and inlabru
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Due to the multitude of ways the point process likelihood can be implemented, E.g. with different integration schemes, and with different normalisation constants, one should not rely on raw DIC values. At best, differences in DIC between two models with _exactly_ the same likelihood implementation should be comparable.

 In your inla vs inlabru comparison, you probably used a different likelihood construction than the defaults of inlabru, explaining the difference.

In addition, the specific way in which the DIC values are computed/estimated can also make a difference. I hope to write more about this after going through the inla code and also doing the math properly for the different likelihood approximations.

Finn

Thank you for sharing the link of ZAP Inlabru. I think I am going to recode the mode using Inlabru packed. In all the examples I have seen online so far about INLAbru, it looks like the data input format is sf or raster format, so I was wondering if it is possible to input data using a data frame format holding lon/lat for each point?

Thank you very much
Morgane

> On Wed, 21 Feb 2024 at 17:56, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > Hi,
> > I haven’t followed this discussion, but for zap model example code, see https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/zip_zap_models.html

> >
> > > On 21 Feb 2024, at 18:03, Tim Meehan <tme...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > ﻿
> > > Hi Morgane,
> > >
> > > I am not sure how to do that. I'll look into ZAP models. In the meantime, maybe someone else
> > > can help? You essentially need a way to simulate counts from your model, using posterior samples
> > > analogous to lambda and p, for the locations where you have counts, and put them into a matrix
> > > for the createDHARMa() function.
> > >
> > > Best,
> > > Tim
> > >
> > > ------------------------------------------------------
> > > Hi Tim
> > >
> > > Thank you very much for getting back to me. Sorry, I have been away for a while.
> > > I tried your last code on the ZIP, and it works =) So thank you very much.
> > > However, I am running a ZAP model composed of binary and zero-inflated parts.
> > > Could you guide me on how to adapt your code to ZAP, which also has a mesh to account for spatial autocorrelation?
> > >
> > > Thank you very much in advance
> > > Morgane
> > >
> > > On Tuesday, February 6, 2024 at 2:21:34 PM UTC-7 Tim Meehan wrote:
> > > > OK, here is a way to do it with all posterior samples, rather than using inla.rmarginal().
> > > >
> > > > # make data
> > > > n <- 100
> > > > p <- 0.75
> > > >
> > > > lam <- 2
> > > > y <- rpois(n, lambda = lam)
> > > > y[rbinom(n, size=1, prob=p) == 1] = 0
> > > > dat1 <- data.frame(y=y)
> > > >
> > > > # make model
> > > > mod1 <- inla(y ~ 1,
> > > >              family = "zeroinflatedpoisson1",
> > > >              data = dat1,
> > > >              control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
> > > >              control.compute=list(config=TRUE))
> > > > summary(mod1)
> > > >
> > > > # get posterior samples of p and lambda
> > > > ss1 <- 50
> > > > samps1 <- inla.posterior.sample(ss1, mod1)
> > > > get_p <- function(...){return(theta[1])}
> > > > sim_p <- inla.posterior.sample.eval(get_p, samps1)
> > > > sim_lam <- exp(inla.posterior.sample.eval("Predictor", samps1))
> > > >
> > > > # use p and lambda samples to simulate counts
> > > > out_sim <- sim_lam
> > > > for(i in 1:nrow(sim_lam)){
> > > >   for(j in 1:ncol(sim_lam)){
> > > >     p <- sim_p[,j]
> > > >
> > > >     p <- 1 - p
> > > >     y <- rpois(1, sim_lam[i,j])
> > > >     y <- y * rbinom(n=1, size=1, prob=p)
> > > >     out_sim[i, j] <- y
> > > >
> > > >   }
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > # run diagnostics in DHARMa
> > > > res <- createDHARMa(simulatedResponse=out_sim,
> > > >                     observedResponse=dat1$y,
> > > >                     integerResponse = T)
> > > > plot(res)
> > > >
> > > > On Tuesday, February 6, 2024 at 11:58:21 AM UTC-7 Tim Meehan wrote:
> > > > > Note, there is probably a better way to pull the expectation for lambda and p at the same time,
> > > > > and transform to simulated counts, using inla.posterior.sample.eval(). But I am still learning
> > > > > the different clever ways to use that function. Maybe someone else can show us how.
> > > > >

> > > > > > n <- 100
> > > > > > p <- 0.8
> > > > > > lam <- 2
> > > > > > y <- rpois(n, lambda = lam)
> > > > > > y[rbinom(n, size=1, prob=p) == 1] = 0
> > > > > > dat1 <- data.frame(y=y)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # make model
> > > > > > mod1 <- inla(y ~ 1,

> > > > > > summary(mod1)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # get posterior samples of expectations and transforms to simulated counts

> > > > > > sim1 <- inla.posterior.sample.eval("Predictor", sim1)
> > > > > > sim1 <- exp(sim1) # need exponentiation
> > > > > > marg1 <- mod1$marginals.hyperpar$`zero-probability parameter for zero-inflated poisson_1`
> > > > > > poi <- function(x, marg){
> > > > > >   p <- inla.rmarginal(1, marg)
> > > > > >   p <- 1 - p
> > > > > >   y <- rpois(1, x)
> > > > > >   y <- y * rbinom(1, size=1, prob=p)
> > > > > >   return(y)
> > > > > > }
> > > > > > sim1 <- apply(sim1, c(1, 2), poi, marg=marg1)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # run diagnostics in DHARMa

> > > > > >                     observedResponse=dat1$y,
> > > > > >                     integerResponse = T)
> > > > > > plot(res)
> > > > > >

> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Best,
> > > > > > > Tim

> > > > > > > --------------------
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Hello Tim,
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Thank you very much for your answer and for correcting the example code I sent. I reall appreciate it.
> > > > > > > To be a bit more precise, I am trying to simulate and use Dhama on the below-fitted model.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > fit = inla(AllY ~ -1 + Intercept.pos + PEA.pos + max_chla.pos +  f(wpos, model = spde) +
> > > > > > >       Intercept.01 + PEA.01 + max_chla.01 + f(w01, model = spde),family = c("zeroinflatedpoisson0", "binomial"),
> > > > > > >       control.family = list(list(hyper = HyperZap),

> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > summary(fit)
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > but then when I run this below code I end up with the following error message
> > > > > > > sim <- inla.posterior.sample(fit) Error in inla.posterior.sample(fit) : !missing(result) && inherits(result, "inla") is not TRUE
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > and I am not sure how to proceed
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Thank you very much
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Morgane
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Monday, February 5, 2024 at 4:11:25 PM UTC-7 Tim Meehan wrote:
> > > > > > > > Hi Morgane,
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > I am not able to answer all your questions at the moment. But to get you started, there were some bugs in the example code you linked to. Here is some running code for a simple Poisson example.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Best,
> > > > > > > > Tim
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > # set up
> > > > > > > > library(INLA)
> > > > > > > > library(DHARMa)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > # make data
> > > > > > > > dat = createData(sampleSize = 500, randomEffectVariance = 0)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > # fit model
> > > > > > > > fit = inla(observedResponse ~ 1 + Environment1 , family = "poisson",
> > > > > > > >            data = dat,
> > > > > > > >            control.family=list(link='log'),
> > > > > > > >            control.predictor=list(link=1, compute=TRUE),
> > > > > > > >            control.compute=list(config = TRUE))
> > > > > > > > summary(fit)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > # get and transform posterior samples
> > > > > > > > sim <- inla.posterior.sample(50, fit)
> > > > > > > > sim <- inla.posterior.sample.eval("Predictor", sim)
> > > > > > > > sim <- exp(sim) # need to exponentiate
> > > > > > > > poi <- function(x){
> > > > > > > >   x = ifelse(x<0, 0, x)
> > > > > > > >   rpois(1, x)
> > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > sim <- apply(sim, c(1,2), poi)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > # run diagnostics
> > > > > > > > res <- createDHARMa(simulatedResponse=sim,
> > > > > > > >                     observedResponse=dat$observedResponse)
> > > > > > > > plot(res)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > On Monday, February 5, 2024 at 5:13:26 AM UTC-7 Morgane Declerck wrote:
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Hi Everyone,
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > I am building a zero-inflated INLA model with spatial autocorrelation to assess seabird distribution. Could anyone guide me on how to use it, or if someone has already used it and would be willing to share the code? Attached please are my data and graphs to analyse.

Yes, it’s possible. However, for spatial modelling, even though the data might have long/lat information, modellinformation should normalt be done in a more sugtabletter local projection to avoid implicit axis-aligned anisotropy; long and lat angles correspond to different length units depending on the location…
But that being said, using “cbind(long, lat)” instead of “geometry” is allowed by the software; it’s just up to you to choose your model…
Finn

Hi,

It’s not clear exactly what you’re asking; the inlabru generate() function internally calls inla.posterior.sample(), and either returns the samples of the model parameters and latent variables, or returns samples of a computed prediction expression.

Since you mention “seed” I’m guessing the issue is to get repeatable samples? To the extent that this is possible with inla.posterior.sample, you must set _both_ the R seed with set.seed(), _and_ the seed argument, as inla uses both R random numbers and its own internal generator.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi Virgilio,

I think I understand; you want to generate and store samples of the
parameters and latent vectors _without_ computing the component
effects, and then _later_ compute the component effects and predictor
expressions?
Yes, if you look at the code for generate.bru(), you'll see that it
first generates the samples, and then only if a predictor formula has
been provided, calls evaluate_model() with "newdata" to evaluate the
component effects, and compute the predictor expression. You could do
the same at a later stage by _not_ providing a formula to generate,
and then later directly calling evaluate_model() in the same way as
generate.bru() does, using the generate() output as "state".

For completeness: the bru predict() method simply calls generate(),
and then a method that computes summary statistics. I plan to make
that summarisation function a supported exported method as well, but
currently that's a more internal part of the predict() function
itself.

"Chunking" the generate() behaviour is something I've wanted to do for
a long time, including using recursive quantile estimation methods in
predict(), to allow a smaller memory footprint when using a large
number of samples, but splitting the parameter/component generation
from the effect&predictor computation I hadn't really considered, even
though as said above is something that should simply work, by doing
exactly what generate does when you do supply a formula and "newdata".

Finn

messages.body_plain:
In the ZIP&ZAG vignette, we run a joint Bernouilli&zero-truncated Poisson (though these could in some cases be run independently), do one could certainly do that; just use generate() instead of predict() in inlabru, to get direct access to the posterior samples of the predictor (and/or directly sample from the data level inside the predictor expression given to generate(), but doing that as a separate step may be easier to code perhaps; we use the sample-inside-predict approach in a few of the inlabru vignettes).
Finn

> On 28 Feb 2024, at 08:39, 'high...@highstat.com' via R-inla discussion group <r-inla-disc...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
>
> ﻿

> Why not (i) run a Bernoulli model,  (ii) a zero-truncated Poisson model, (iii) pass on the pi and mu to VGAM (it has a function to simulate ZAG data for given pi and mu), (iv)  use the INLA facilities for posterior simulation to do this 1000 times, and (v) pass this on to DHARMa? Not very difficult to do. It does assume that the two components of the model are independent, though.
>

messages.body_plain:
I've checked the code now.
generate.bru calls evaluate_model with

vals <- evaluate_model(
      model = object$bru_info$model,
      state = state,
      data = newdata,
      predictor = formula,
      used = used
    )

which doesn't use the "input" argument. The "input" argument to
evaluate_model() may be used elsewhere in the code where
evaluate_model is called repeatedly for individual state vectors, to
avoid having to recompute the "input" values when the data/newdata
remains unchanged. In your use case, you will supply different data
each time, so it wouldn't benefit from having that precomputed.

Finn

Dear Professor Krainski,

First of all, I offer you my apologies because I just noticed that I didn't respond to your last contribution, which was very helpful. Thank you very much.

I'm revisiting this problem after a few months. Despite thinking that I can create a model using real data if I follow your valuable instructions, I'm looking to run a simulation first. Studying your example in Chapter 5 of "Advanced Spatial Modeling with Stochastic Partial Differential Equations Using R and INLA," I noticed that you obtained precise estimations of theta parameters. I also consulted the article "Bayesian Spatial Modelling with R-INLA" by Professor Finn, and they got precise estimations too. I need to combine the inclusion of a covariate in the SPDE model (present in your book) with the definition of the response variable as a linear model (present in Professor Finn's article). To do this, I'm adapting an example from "Spatial and Spatio-temporal Bayesian Models with R-INLA" (page 229). I am obtaining pretty bad results if I use non-informative priors (which also happens in the book), so I'm wondering if there is something wrong in the code or if the lack of precision is a consequence of the greater complexity of the model. Again, your help will be appreciated.

I'm aware that the selection of hyperparameters values is crucial in this kind of model, and the ones I'm using (corresponding to the original paper) are not proper for the selected data, but I'm also sure that there are other silly mistakes. I will appreciate it if you can point these out for me in order to achieve the estimation. I will also appreciate any recommendations for the selection of hyperparameter values, considering that the original priors are very informative. Thank you in advance for your help an guidance.
